evidence: src/infrastructure/http/controllers/OrderController.ts: class OrderController handlers (place, list, get, pay, pack, ship, deliver, cancel) each forward to this.useCases.<x>.execute(...) and send the result with res.json; parsing goes through parsePlaceOrderBody and parseStateQuery from ../requestParsing

src/infrastructure/http/controllers/StockController.ts: class StockController handlers list/get forward to listProductStock.execute() and getProductStock.execute(req.params.id) and send the result with res.json, the same adapter pattern

Style difference only: OrderController injects one OrderUseCases object and uses a named `type IdParams = { id: string }`. StockController injects ListProductStockUseCase and GetProductStockUseCase separately and writes `Request<{ id: string }>` inline. No business rule is duplicated.
Neither file contains domain logic or validation that should live elsewhere. Both delegate fully to the application use cases.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: Both files cover one concern: they are thin Express adapters that turn HTTP requests into application use-case calls and send back JSON. Neither file holds domain rules or invariants. Request parsing is kept in one place, the shared ../requestParsing module (parsePlaceOrderBody, parseStateQuery), and is not repeated. StockController does no body or query parsing, so it has nothing to call there. Both controllers follow the same pattern: arrow-function handlers on a class, constructor-injected use cases, and `.execute(...)` followed by `res.json`. There are two small style differences. OrderController receives its use cases as one OrderUseCases object, while StockController takes two separate constructor parameters. OrderController also uses a named IdParams type where StockController writes `{ id: string }` inline. These are differences in how dependencies are passed, not a duplicated rule or invariant, and neither file goes around a module abstraction. That does not meet the fail criteria.
